title: Who checked, and how
happened: The proof was published as a Lean formalisation split into a 14-part compressed archive, linked from a footnote of the note. Members checked what they could. One downloaded it and reported it unpacks to 1.4 GB of Lean. Others joked that the real explanation would be a bug in Lean, and that if Lean is fine then mathematics itself is inconsistent. When colin-fraser said the hypothesis has a standard Lean statement and it would be surprising if that was not used, shibbi replied that it was, he had checked, that there were no 'sorry' escape hatches, and posted a summary saying none across 175,187 files; sciortino replied that this makes it double extra definitely proved. In the evening davidcrespo and scanstone posted a screenshot from the Lean community's Zulip chat in which a mathematician reported that an independent Lean kernel had accepted the proof, after which norvid asked why Lean uses Zulip rather than Discord, and what 'lake comparator paranoid' is. Others said they would buy compute just to compile such proof dumps, or trusted that enough 'turbonerds' were checking. A member proposed a Bayesian paper on whether the proof adds anything to numerical evidence; another said he'd have Claude prove Lean itself and was told it had been done. Asked by a non-member how the answer is shown to be correct, zachweinersmith replied with one word: Lean. And catblanketflower asked her magic 8-ball bot whether the proof would hold up; it said 'Yes definitely.', and she said 'whew'. Many of those checking said plainly that they could not judge it themselves. The show can assert nothing about whether the proof (or the human proof mentioned here) is correct; on 20 November it was a claim being checked, and these posts are people reacting to the claim.

alts:
• No escape hatches. Across all 175,187 files there are zero sorry s, admit s, custom axiomS, opaque S, native_decide S, implemented_bys, unsafes, or kernel-skipping options. Nothing redefines riemannZeta, LFunction or
RiemannHypothesis through notation or macros. The only environment-modifying commands add names to a tactic-suggestion deny list, which can't change what the kernel accepts.
• Mathlib is pinned to one exact commit, so the definitions it relies on can't drift.

# What I couldn't confirm:
• That it builds. The main theorem pulls in every one of the 175k files: 17.4 million lines, about nine times the size of Mathlib, on Lean 4.33.1. This machine has 2 cores and 7 GB of RAM. Realistically it needs a big multi-core box for a day or so, plus the Mathlib build cache

alts:
Screenshot of a dark-mode chat message from Andrew Sutherland at 1:09 PM with 37 party popper reactions:

First independent-kernel verdict: nanoda accepts the proof.

nanoda (the Rust kernel, Lean 4.36.0’s bundled nanoda_bin) checked the full 61.57 GB export and exited 0 at 2:05:45 PM EST. Wall time 27 min 42 s on 80 threads, about 9.2 CPU-hours, peak memory 89 GB. The export it read has the expected sha256 5ea74b91...244e.

Statement comparison and axiom check passed in the lake comparator --paranoid run: it got through both and moved on to its first kernel ("Running Lean paranoid kernel on solution"). Caveat: that run used my earlier challenge export, which differs from the canonical one only in sorry placeholders; the run with the canonical challenge started at 2:03 PM EST and is still parsing.

alts:
Summary

The published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, and the independent nanoda kernel accepts the full exported proof. The lake comparator run and the Lean-kernel replay of the export are still in progress.
